newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's Socialists stick to guns on new cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's Socialists stick to guns on new cabinet.

text.p: Bulgaria's ruling Socialists refused to give way on Friday to a chorus of demands for early elections by clowning students, striking workers, angry marchers and an exiled king.

The former communists, unmoved by a 12th day of popular unrest, stuck to their insistence on forming a new cabinet but said talks with the opposition could resume when president-elect Petar Stoyanov was sworn in on Sunday.
The opposition is boycotting parliament until its demands are met but has said it will attend Sunday's inauguration.
"We shall use the opportunity of the participation of our colleagues on January 19 to invite them again for talks," Socialist Party leader Georgi Parvanov said on Friday.
Thousands took to the streets of Sofia again to demonstrate against economic misery and for general elections, not constitutionally required for almost another two years.
Ever seeking novel forms of protest, several students abseiled down the wall of a university building and one marched in a skeleton costume to represent the "death" of Bulgaria.
A rash of one-hour protest strikes was reported nationwide. King Simeon II, who fled Bulgaria as a child in 1946 after the communist takeover, added his voice to demands for elections.
"We are all witness to what Bulgaria was turned into by mediocrity, egoism, greed and hunger for power," Simeon, a Madrid-based business consultant, said in a statement.
Sofia demonstrators on Friday carried portraits of the king, greeted rapturously on his first return to Bulgaria last May, and sang the monarchist-era national anthem.
With inflation at 300 percent and incomes plunging, the opposition calls the government both incompetent and corrupt.

"Dialogue...is very difficult as there are some people within the Socialist Party for whom to leave the parliament means to be prosecuted, not for political reasons but for criminal actions," Nadezhda Mihailova of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) told a news conference.

The opposition could not agree to the Socialists' demand to form a new cabinet, she said. Outgoing president Zhelyu Zhelev, a fierce critic, has refused to ask them to form a government but Stoyanov has said he is prepared to do so.
UDF leader Ivan Kostov urged 20,000 protesters in Sofia on Friday to emulate the marathon protests in Belgrade.
"We should look to our friends in Serbia and see how they manage to achieve a success with their constant protests," he said. "We not going to agree to a second Socialist government."

The Socialists have proposed elections by the end of the year but the UDF wants them sooner, and insists that parliament vote on its Declaration for National Salvation, which was at the root of a 10-hour siege of parliament a week ago.
It calls for general elections, a new central bank board to implement a fixed exchange rate regime, and an all-party team to negotiate with the IMF on a programme to save the economy.
The IMF said it would complete stalled talks on a currency board with a new government as soon as one was appointed.

"Bulgaria is in a state of weightlessness. There is no government, no budget, the finance minister is on the way out and the legitimacy of the central bank is becoming dubious," co-manager of Adlon-Discont brokerage house Andrei Pramov told Reuters.

An opinion poll published on Thursday put support for the Socialists at just eight percent but said UDF support had not changed since November's presidential election, suggesting the motives for the protests were economic rather than political.
Diplomats said later elections would help the Socialists if held after a new IMF accord and reforms began to bear fruit.
The collapsing lev currency fell to new lows below 700 to the dollar on the interbank market on Friday. The daily Kontinent said lev coins were now worth more as scrap metal.
The IMF has said one of its main concerns was the level of corruption. Outgoing prime minister Zhan Videnov came under fire for links to a group of companies known as Orion.
Students appealed for an investigation into powerful business groups and their relations with politicians.

"Future parliamentary candidates should sign declarations that they are not and never have been linked, through business or otherwise, with the power, insurance and security firms and economic groupings which violate the law," a statement said.
